title: Abstract Factory Pattern
tagline: Create families of related objects without specifying their concrete classes — ensuring that objects from one family are never mixed with objects from another.

sections.content:
Imagine you are building a cross-platform UI toolkit. You have `Button`, `Checkbox`, `Dialog`, and `Tooltip` components that must all render correctly on both macOS and Windows. A naive implementation scatters `new MacButton()` and `new WindowsCheckbox()` throughout the codebase. Someone eventually combines a Mac button with a Windows checkbox — the UI looks wrong, the styles clash, and you have a correctness bug that is hard to detect until a user files a report.

The deeper issue is not a bug in any single file — it is an **architectural gap**: nothing in the system prevents cross-family mixing. You need a structure that makes inconsistency impossible by construction, not just by convention.

**The Abstract Factory pattern** is exactly that structure. It defines an interface for creating an entire **family of related products** — one creation method per product type. Each concrete factory implements the full interface for one family. Client code receives a factory via injection, calls its creation methods, and gets a complete, consistent set of products — never knowing or caring which concrete family it received.

**What you will understand after this chapter:** the five participants of Abstract Factory and their exact roles, how family consistency is guaranteed by structure rather than discipline, how Abstract Factory relates to Factory Method, how to implement it in JavaScript and TypeScript, when it genuinely earns its complexity overhead, real-world frameworks that rely on it, and the precise trade-offs that should make you reach for a simpler pattern instead.

**The key insight up front:** Abstract Factory solves a *family consistency* problem. If you do not have multiple product families that must be used together, this pattern is overkill. When you do have that problem, Abstract Factory is the cleanest known solution.

sections.caption: UIFactory declares one creation method per product type. MacFactory and WinFactory each implement every method, guaranteeing a coherent set of products. Client code depends only on UIFactory, Button, and Checkbox — never on MacButton or WinCheckbox directly.

sections.title: The Furniture Showroom and the Coordinated Collection
sections.content:
An interior designer is hired to furnish a corporate office in a consistent style — the client insists on either a **Modern** look or a **Victorian** look, but not a mixture. The designer does not wander a warehouse picking random pieces. Instead, they place a single call to either the *Modern Furniture Supplier* or the *Victorian Furniture Supplier*. That supplier provides a sofa, an armchair, and a coffee table — all from the same collection, all matching in material, colour, and proportion.

If the client changes their mind and wants Victorian, the designer simply switches suppliers. Every piece changes as a coordinated set — there is no risk of a Modern glass coffee table sitting next to a Victorian tufted sofa, because the supplier selection prevents the mix.

The Abstract Factory is the supplier contract: you call `supplier.orderSofa()`, `supplier.orderChair()`, `supplier.orderTable()` — and however the supplier is implemented, you are guaranteed all three pieces belong to the same family. The concrete supplier (Modern or Victorian) is injected at the start; every subsequent call honours that commitment.

In software: replace 'furniture collection' with 'UI theme', 'database dialect', or 'test-double set', and replace 'interior designer' with 'application client'. The pattern is the same.

sections.title: The Five Participants and Their Exact Roles
sections.content:
Abstract Factory has five named participants. Understanding what each one *owns* is the key to applying the pattern correctly.

**1. AbstractFactory** — the interface (or abstract class) that declares one creation method per product type in the family. In TypeScript this is a `interface` with methods like `createButton(): Button`. In JavaScript it is a class whose methods `throw new Error('not implemented')`. Client code depends on this interface only — it never references a concrete factory class.

**2. ConcreteFactory** (e.g. `MacFactory`, `WinFactory`, `DarkThemeFactory`) — implements AbstractFactory. It is responsible for creating the complete product set for *one* family. Each method is itself a **Factory Method** — it encapsulates the `new ConcreteProduct()` call that the client must never see. A system with three families has three concrete factories; adding a fourth family adds one more concrete factory.

**3. AbstractProduct** — the interface for each individual product type (`Button`, `Checkbox`, `Tooltip`). Clients work with these interfaces, never with concrete types. A family with three product types has three abstract product interfaces.

**4. ConcreteProduct** — a specific product belonging to a specific family (`MacButton`, `WinButton`, `DarkThemeCheckbox`). A system with three families and three product types has nine concrete product classes. Each implements one AbstractProduct interface and belongs to exactly one family.

**5. Client** — uses only the AbstractFactory interface to obtain products, and uses only AbstractProduct interfaces to work with them. The concrete family the client receives is determined entirely by which ConcreteFactory is injected — the client has zero if-statements, zero `instanceof` checks, and zero knowledge of concrete types.

**End-to-end flow:** at application startup, a configuration mechanism (OS detection, environment variable, user setting, DI container) selects and instantiates the appropriate ConcreteFactory. That factory is injected into every client component that needs to create products. Each client calls the factory's creation methods, stores the results behind their AbstractProduct interfaces, and uses them freely — the concrete family is fully transparent.

sections.title: Abstract Factory vs. Factory Method — Understanding the Relationship
sections.content:
These two patterns are often confused because their names share a word. The difference is precise.

**Factory Method** solves a single-product problem: a superclass defines a method for creating *one* product, and subclasses override that method to change the concrete type. There is one product type, one creation method per subclass. The pattern is about deferring instantiation of a single product to a subclass decision.

**Abstract Factory** solves a *multi-product family* problem: an interface declares multiple creation methods, one per product type. Each concrete factory implements all of them, producing a coherent family. The pattern is about guaranteeing that multiple different products come from the same family.

**Abstract Factory is typically implemented using Factory Methods.** Each creation method on a concrete factory (`MacFactory.createButton()`, `MacFactory.createCheckbox()`) is, by definition, a Factory Method — it encapsulates a concrete `new` call behind an interface. Abstract Factory is a *suite* of coordinated Factory Methods that work together to guarantee family consistency. Factory Method is a single instrument; Abstract Factory is an orchestra.

**A useful heuristic:** if you catch yourself thinking 'I need to swap out one product type', reach for Factory Method. If you find yourself thinking 'I need to swap out an entire set of related products', reach for Abstract Factory.

**Builder pattern comparison:** Builder is also often confused with Abstract Factory. Builder constructs a single complex object step-by-step, allowing different configurations of the same type (a House can have a garage or not, two or four windows). Abstract Factory creates multiple distinct product types that form a family. The output of Builder is always one thing; the output of Abstract Factory is a coordinated set of things.

sections.caption: Factory Method and Abstract Factory operate at different scopes. Abstract Factory is the higher-level pattern that coordinates multiple Factory Methods into a coherent family creation interface.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: Three families, three product types — nine concrete classes, but `LoginForm` references none of them. When `HighContrastThemeFactory` was added, not a single line of `LoginForm`, `LightThemeFactory`, `DarkThemeFactory`, or any Abstract Product changed. The registry is the only extension point — and even that can be replaced by a DI container. This is Open/Closed Principle applied at the family level.

sections.title: TypeScript Implementation — Interfaces Over Base Classes
sections.content:
JavaScript's dynamic typing means you can implement Abstract Factory with base classes that throw errors, but **TypeScript gives you true compile-time enforcement** through interfaces. This is often the preferred approach in production TypeScript codebases.

With TypeScript interfaces, the compiler catches missing creation methods on a ConcreteFactory *before* the code ever runs. You get autocomplete, refactoring safety, and documentation for free.

The TypeScript approach uses `interface` for both the AbstractFactory and all AbstractProduct types. ConcreteFactory classes `implement` the factory interface. The compiler enforces that every creation method is present and returns the correct abstract type.

A common enhancement is to combine Abstract Factory with **TypeScript's discriminated unions** for product families, making it easy to add exhaustive checks when the family is known at a specific point. However, most Abstract Factory implementations keep the family opaque to clients — the factory is received via a parameter typed as the abstract factory interface, and the concrete family never leaks through.

**Dependency Injection containers** (like InversifyJS, tsyringe, or NestJS's built-in DI) pair naturally with Abstract Factory. You register the ConcreteFactory against the AbstractFactory token, and the DI container injects the right family everywhere that token appears. Switching families in tests becomes a single line of DI configuration — the canonical use of Abstract Factory for test infrastructure.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: TypeScript's `implements` keyword gives compile-time verification that every ConcreteFactory covers every creation method. `UserRepository` has no `import` for `PgQueryBuilder` or `SqliteQueryBuilder` — those names appear nowhere in the client file. Switching between databases in tests is a single constructor argument. This is the canonical test-infrastructure use of Abstract Factory.

sections.title: The Family Consistency Guarantee — Why It Matters
sections.content:
The central promise of Abstract Factory is the **family consistency guarantee**: if all products in a system are created by the same factory instance, they are guaranteed to belong to the same family and therefore to be compatible with each other.

This is not just a good practice — it is a structural property. Consider the alternative: a client that creates products by calling `new MacButton()` and `new WinCheckbox()` directly must rely on developer discipline to avoid mixing families. Add another developer, add time pressure, add a refactoring that renames a class, and the discipline breaks down. Bugs appear.

With Abstract Factory, cross-family mixing is **impossible by construction**. The factory interface simply does not offer a method that creates a Mac button alongside a Windows checkbox. To get products from two different families, you would need two different factory instances — and the client is designed to hold only one. The pattern encodes the constraint directly into the type system.

**Why does this matter in practice?**

- **UI theming systems:** a component library must guarantee that all icons, buttons, inputs, and modals in a given render pass use the same colour tokens, spacing scale, and border radii. Mixing themes produces visual glitches that are hard to reproduce and trace.
- **Database dialect layers:** a query builder, connection pool, and migration runner must all speak the same SQL dialect. Mixing PostgreSQL query syntax with an SQLite connection crashes at runtime with cryptic errors.
- **Test infrastructure:** production services and test doubles must form consistent sets. If a test injects a real HTTP client but a fake database, timing and teardown bugs appear. The test double factory guarantees the entire set of dependencies is either all-real or all-fake.
- **Payment provider SDKs:** a payment processor's request signer, response parser, and webhook validator must all use the same cryptographic scheme and data format. Mixing Stripe's parser with Braintree's signer produces silent data corruption.

The pattern's value is directly proportional to how badly cross-family mixing would hurt you.

sections.title: The Extensibility Trade-off — New Families vs. New Product Types
sections.content:
Abstract Factory has a well-known asymmetry in its extensibility, and understanding it determines whether the pattern is the right tool for a given problem.

**Adding a new family is easy and OCP-safe.** Creating a `HighContrastThemeFactory` requires: one new factory class, one new concrete product class per product type. No existing code changes — not the AbstractFactory interface, not existing concrete factories, not client code. This is the pattern's sweet spot.

**Adding a new product type is hard and violates OCP for existing factories.** Suppose you realise the theming system needs a `Tooltip` in addition to `Button`, `Input`, and `Card`. You must: add `createTooltip()` to the AbstractFactory interface, implement `createTooltip()` in *every existing ConcreteFactory* (`LightThemeFactory`, `DarkThemeFactory`, `HighContrastThemeFactory`), and create a corresponding ConcreteProduct for each family. Every existing concrete factory must be opened and edited — a direct OCP violation.

**The strategic implication:** use Abstract Factory when your product types are stable and your families are likely to grow. If you expect to frequently add new product types, consider a different decomposition — perhaps a simpler registry pattern or explicit configuration objects.

**Mitigation strategies for the product-type extension problem:**

1. *Default implementations on the base class* — if AbstractFactory is a base class rather than an interface, new methods can be given a default implementation (e.g. a generic tooltip) that existing factories inherit. Only families that need a custom tooltip override it. This breaks strict interface segregation but reduces the blast radius of adding new product types.

2. *Separate factories for extension points* — divide the factory interface into stable and unstable parts. `CoreUIFactory` declares the four most stable product types; `ExtendedUIFactory` extends it with newer types. Existing factories only implement `CoreUIFactory` until they are ready.

3. *Prototype-based factories* — instead of `createX()` methods, the factory holds prototype instances and clones them on demand. Adding a product type means adding a property to the factory configuration object — no interface change required. Less type-safe, but more flexible.

sections.title: Common Misconceptions and Edge Cases
sections.content:
**Misconception 1: 'Abstract Factory requires abstract classes.'** No. In JavaScript, any object with the right creation methods can serve as a factory. In TypeScript, `interface` (not `abstract class`) is the preferred tool for the AbstractFactory role. The word 'abstract' in the pattern name refers to the concept of abstracting over a family of products, not to a specific language construct.

**Misconception 2: 'You need a base class for every abstract product.'** Not necessarily. In TypeScript, `interface` is lighter and preferred. In JavaScript, duck typing means the factory's return value just needs to have the right methods — no inheritance required. That said, a shared base class can be useful for providing default implementations and enforcing the interface in plain JS.

**Misconception 3: 'Abstract Factory is just a namespace for constructors.'** This misses the point. The pattern's value is injection and substitutability. A module that exports `{ MacButton, MacCheckbox }` as a namespace does not give you the ability to inject a different family. The factory is a runtime object — it can be swapped, mocked, configured, or serialised.

**Misconception 4: 'One Abstract Factory per application.'** The pattern can appear multiple times in a codebase for different concerns. A UI theming factory and a database adapter factory can coexist independently. Each solves family consistency for its own domain.

**Misconception 5: 'The client must not know anything about families.'** This is the goal, not an absolute rule. Sometimes a factory selector function — `getFactory(config)` — needs to know the concrete factory names to build the registry. That code is the composition root, not the client. The client code downstream of the composition root remains ignorant of concrete types.

**Edge case — singleton factories:** Often, each ConcreteFactory should be a singleton (or at least instantiated once). Creating a new `MacFactory()` on every request is wasteful if factory construction is non-trivial. A simple registry object or module-level constant achieves this: `const FACTORIES = { mac: new MacFactory(), win: new WinFactory() }`.

**Edge case — parameterised factories:** Sometimes products need configuration (e.g. a button with a specific label). This can be handled by passing parameters to the `createX()` methods: `factory.createButton({ label: 'Save', variant: 'primary' })`. This is fine and common. The factory still enforces family; it just accepts per-product configuration.

**Edge case — products that reference each other:** In some designs, products from the same family need to collaborate (a mac scroll bar knows how to attach to a mac container). This reinforces the need for family consistency — a cross-family product would fail to collaborate. Inject the factory into products that need to create compatible siblings.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart TD
    AF["AbstractFactory interface"] --> Easy["Adding a new FAMILY"]
    AF --> Hard["Adding a new PRODUCT TYPE"]
    Easy --> E1["New ConcreteFactory class"]
    Easy --> E2["New ConcreteProduct per type"]
    Easy --> E3["Zero existing code changes"]
    Hard --> H1["Update AbstractFactory interface"]
    Hard --> H2["Update ALL ConcreteFactories"]
    Hard --> H3["New ConcreteProduct per family"]
sections.caption: The extensibility asymmetry: new families are OCP-safe (add without modifying). New product types require touching every existing ConcreteFactory. Design your abstraction boundaries around which dimension changes more often.

sections.title: Real-World Frameworks That Use Abstract Factory
sections.content:
Abstract Factory is not an academic exercise — it appears throughout production frameworks and libraries.

**Angular's TestBed** is the canonical test-infrastructure example. The `TestBed.configureTestingModule()` call registers a complete set of test doubles — mock services, fake HTTP backend, in-memory stores — replacing the production family. The component under test depends on Angular's DI token interfaces; `TestBed` injects the test-double family. Adding `HttpClientTestingModule` swaps the entire HTTP family (client, interceptors, backend) in one declaration.

**React's Renderers** follow the same structure. `react-dom` is a factory for browser DOM products (elements, events, effects). `react-test-renderer` is a factory for in-memory test products. `react-native` is a factory for native view products. The React component tree calls `createElement` — the abstract creation method — and the renderer determines what concrete 'product' results. Switching from browser to test or native rendering is switching the renderer (factory), not the component code.

**Database ORM dialect layers** in libraries like TypeORM, Sequelize, and Knex use Abstract Factory internally. Each supported database (PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, MSSQL) has a dialect factory that produces a query builder, schema builder, and migration runner compatible with that database. The ORM client calls the abstract query builder and never references `PgQueryBuilder` directly.

**MUI (Material-UI)'s theming system** produces a family of styled components from a theme configuration. `createTheme()` is effectively the abstract factory call; the returned theme object is the factory. `ThemeProvider` injects it; every MUI component calls `useTheme()` to get the factory-produced styling. Switching from default to dark mode swaps the theme (factory), and all components update consistently.

**Java's JDBC architecture** is a textbook Abstract Factory. `DriverManager.getConnection()` returns a `Connection` (abstract product). `Connection.createStatement()` returns a `Statement`; `Connection.prepareStatement()` returns a `PreparedStatement`. Each JDBC driver (PostgreSQL driver, MySQL Connector/J, H2) provides a concrete factory (the Driver) that produces a complete, consistent family of JDBC objects. Application code uses only JDBC interfaces; the driver jar is swapped without changing a line of application code.

**Historical context:** The Abstract Factory pattern was first formally named in the landmark 1994 book *Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software* (Gamma, Helm, Johnson, Vlissides — the 'Gang of Four'). The motivating example in the original text was exactly a cross-platform widget toolkit (Motif vs. Presentation Manager), which maps almost perfectly to modern UI theming problems. The 30-year relevance of the same example is a testament to how fundamental the pattern's problem is. The GoF called it 'Kit' as an alternative name, emphasising the idea of a coordinated toolkit of components.

**When to reach for Abstract Factory:** your system supports multiple product families that must be used together; products from different families are incompatible; you want to swap the entire family at a single configuration point; you are building test infrastructure that needs to replace a whole set of production dependencies with test doubles.

**When NOT to use it:** you only have one product type (Factory Method is simpler); you only have one family (plain constructors or a single factory function is enough); your product types are still evolving rapidly (the update-every-factory cost is painful early); the team is small and family mixing is not a realistic risk (the complexity overhead buys nothing).

**The class explosion warning:** a system with F families and P product types produces F×P concrete product classes plus F concrete factory classes. Three families with five product types = 15 concrete products + 3 factories = 18 new classes. This is the pattern's primary cost. Consider whether TypeScript interfaces + discriminated unions or a configuration-object approach can solve the same problem with less ceremony before committing to the full pattern.

items: **Family consistency is the core guarantee** — all products created by one factory instance are guaranteed to be from the same family; cross-family mixing is impossible by construction, not merely discouraged by convention.

**Five participants work together** — AbstractFactory, ConcreteFactory, AbstractProduct, ConcreteProduct, and Client each have a precise role; the client depends only on the abstract types, making the concrete family fully substitutable.

**Abstract Factory is a suite of Factory Methods** — each creation method on a ConcreteFactory is itself a Factory Method; Abstract Factory coordinates several Factory Methods to produce a coherent product set for one family.

**Extensibility is asymmetric** — adding a new family (new ConcreteFactory + ConcreteProducts) is OCP-safe and requires zero existing-code changes; adding a new product type requires updating every ConcreteFactory — design boundaries around which dimension changes more often.

**Injection is the delivery mechanism** — the concrete factory is selected once at the composition root (startup, DI container, test setup) and injected into clients; no client ever calls `new ConcreteProduct()` directly.

**Real frameworks rely on it** — Angular TestBed, React renderers, ORM dialect layers, MUI theming, and JDBC all use Abstract Factory to make families of related components swappable without touching application logic.

**Class explosion is the main cost** — F families × P product types = F×P concrete classes; weigh this against the consistency guarantee and choose a simpler pattern (plain registry, Factory Method, configuration object) when the full pattern's overhead is not justified.

quiz.question: What is the primary problem that Abstract Factory solves?
options: Ensuring a class has only one instance throughout the application lifecycle.
Constructing a single complex object step-by-step with many optional parameters.
Creating families of related objects that must be used together, preventing cross-family mixing.
Deferring the instantiation of a single product type to a subclass override.
quiz.explanation: Abstract Factory guarantees that all products created for a system come from the same family and are therefore mutually compatible. It makes cross-family mixing (e.g. Mac button with Windows checkbox) impossible by construction, not just by convention.

quiz.question: How does Abstract Factory differ from Factory Method?
options: Factory Method creates a family of products; Abstract Factory creates a single product type.
Abstract Factory creates a family of related product types; Factory Method defers creation of one product type to a subclass.
Abstract Factory uses inheritance; Factory Method uses only composition.
There is no meaningful difference — they are the same pattern with different names.
quiz.explanation: Factory Method handles one product type via a single subclass override. Abstract Factory defines multiple creation methods — one per product type — and each ConcreteFactory implements all of them to produce a consistent family. Abstract Factory is often built from multiple Factory Methods coordinated together.

quiz.question: In a TypeScript Abstract Factory, what is the correct role of an `interface` like `ThemeFactory`?
options: It is a ConcreteFactory that clients instantiate directly.
It is the AbstractFactory: it declares one creation method per product type and is what client code depends on.
It is an AbstractProduct that defines the behaviour of one product type.
It is a registry that maps theme names to their concrete factory classes.
quiz.explanation: The `ThemeFactory` interface is the AbstractFactory participant. It declares the creation contract — one method per product type — without implementation. Client code holds a reference typed as `ThemeFactory`, never as `LightThemeFactory` or `DarkThemeFactory`. The compiler enforces that every ConcreteFactory implements every creation method.

quiz.question: A developer adds a `HighContrastThemeFactory` to a system that already has `LightThemeFactory` and `DarkThemeFactory`. Which files must change?
options: The AbstractFactory interface, all existing ConcreteFactories, and all client components.
Only the client components that need to support the new theme.
Only the new HighContrastThemeFactory class and the new HighContrast concrete product classes, plus the factory registry.
All existing ConcreteProduct classes must be updated to handle the new family.
quiz.explanation: Adding a new family is OCP-safe. You create one new ConcreteFactory and one new ConcreteProduct per product type. Existing AbstractFactory interface, existing ConcreteFactories, and all client code remain untouched. Only the factory registry (or DI config) gains a new entry.

quiz.question: What is the main extensibility cost of Abstract Factory?
options: Adding a new family requires editing all existing concrete product classes.
Adding a new product TYPE requires updating every existing ConcreteFactory to implement the new creation method.
The AbstractFactory interface can only declare two creation methods maximum.
Each call to a factory method instantiates multiple objects, causing memory overhead.
quiz.explanation: Adding a new product type (e.g. `createTooltip()`) requires adding the method to the AbstractFactory interface AND implementing it in every existing ConcreteFactory. This is the pattern's main rigidity — it is optimised for adding families, not for adding product types.

quiz.question: A `UserRepository` receives a `DatabaseAdapterFactory` in its constructor and stores `this.qb = factory.createQueryBuilder()`. What is the relationship between `UserRepository` and `PgQueryBuilder`?
options: UserRepository imports PgQueryBuilder and calls its constructor when needed.
UserRepository has no direct dependency on PgQueryBuilder — it only depends on the QueryBuilder interface.
UserRepository uses instanceof checks to detect which concrete QueryBuilder it received.
UserRepository inherits from PgQueryBuilder to get its SQL generation methods.
quiz.explanation: The client (`UserRepository`) depends only on the abstract `QueryBuilder` interface and the abstract `DatabaseAdapterFactory` interface. `PgQueryBuilder` is never imported, referenced, or checked. The concrete type is invisible to the client — this is the core encapsulation benefit of Abstract Factory.

quiz.question: Why is Angular's TestBed considered an example of Abstract Factory in practice?
options: TestBed creates singleton services that persist across the entire test suite.
TestBed replaces the entire family of production dependencies with a consistent set of test doubles — the component under test depends on the same abstract interfaces in both cases.
TestBed uses lazy initialization to avoid creating services until they are first requested.
TestBed caches component instances to speed up test execution.
quiz.explanation: TestBed is a test-infrastructure factory. It provides a consistent family of test doubles (mock services, fake HTTP backend) that replaces the production family. The component under test uses the same Angular DI interfaces in both production and test — only the injected family changes. This is Abstract Factory applied to test infrastructure.

quiz.question: What is the relationship between the methods on a ConcreteFactory and the Factory Method pattern?
options: They have no relationship — Abstract Factory and Factory Method are mutually exclusive patterns.
Each creation method on a ConcreteFactory is itself a Factory Method: it encapsulates a `new ConcreteProduct()` call behind an interface.
Factory Methods are used only by the AbstractFactory, not by ConcreteFactories.
Factory Method pattern replaced Abstract Factory in modern object-oriented design.
quiz.explanation: Every `createX()` method on a ConcreteFactory is a Factory Method — it defines a creation interface that the concrete class implements, hiding the `new ConcreteProduct()` call from the client. Abstract Factory is a suite of coordinated Factory Methods, each producing one product type in the family.

quiz.question: A system has 4 product families and 5 product types. How many ConcreteProduct classes does a full Abstract Factory implementation require?
quiz.explanation: Each of the 4 families needs one ConcreteProduct for each of the 5 product types: 4 × 5 = 20 concrete product classes, plus 4 concrete factory classes. This class explosion (20 + 4 = 24 classes for 9 conceptual types) is the pattern's primary cost and the main reason to evaluate simpler alternatives first.

quiz.question: When is Abstract Factory the WRONG choice?
options: When you need to swap entire product families at a single configuration point.
When building test infrastructure that replaces a complete set of production dependencies.
When you have only one product type to create, or only one family that will ever exist.
When different products in the same family must be guaranteed to be compatible with each other.
quiz.explanation: If you have only one product type, Factory Method is simpler. If you have only one family, plain constructors or a factory function are enough — Abstract Factory's overhead (interface, multiple concrete classes, injection infrastructure) buys nothing when there is nothing to swap. The pattern earns its complexity only when multiple families genuinely exist and consistency matters.
